title: Week 112 · Lesson 136: Pediatric Urinary & Genital Complaints — FNP-Level UTI, Voiding and Torsion Safety
html:
PHASE 5 · FAMILY & LIFESPAN PRIMARY CARE

Week 112 — Lesson 136: Pediatric Urinary & Genital Complaints

FNP-level goal: Evaluate urinary and genital symptoms using age, collection quality, urinalysis, culture, bowel-bladder function, anatomy, and safeguarding context; treat probable infection appropriately; prevent recurrent dysfunction; and recognize testicular torsion, obstructed infection, abuse, and systemic renal disease.

Learning Objectives

  • Recognize age-specific UTI presentations and obtain urine suitable for the clinical question before antibiotics when safe.
  • Interpret urinalysis and culture together while accounting for contamination and collection method.
  • Distinguish cystitis, febrile UTI or pyelonephritis, asymptomatic bacteriuria, vulvovaginitis, balanitis, and dysfunctional voiding.
  • Evaluate enuresis, constipation, hematuria, and proteinuria without unnecessary testing.
  • Identify torsion, urinary obstruction, sepsis, genital trauma, and safeguarding concerns requiring urgent action.

Part 1 — Age Changes the Presentation

Infants with UTI may have fever, poor feeding, vomiting, jaundice, irritability, or poor growth without dysuria. Older children may report frequency, urgency, dysuria, suprapubic pain, flank pain, or new incontinence. Adolescents require confidential assessment of sexual exposure, pregnancy possibility, urethritis, pelvic infection, and safety.

Begin with appearance, temperature, hydration, perfusion, blood pressure when indicated, abdominal or flank tenderness, urine output, and ability to take fluids. A toxic child, young infant with fever, obstructed or absent urine, severe dehydration, or sepsis concern requires urgent evaluation.

Part 2 — Focused History

Ask timing, fever, urinary frequency and volume, pain, urgency, odor, blood, flank or abdominal pain, vomiting, prior culture results, antibiotics, anomalies, stones, catheterization, constipation, withholding, daytime wetting, stream quality, polydipsia, weight loss, edema, rash, trauma, and family renal history.

For genital symptoms, ask itch, discharge, lesions, bleeding, hygiene products, tight clothing, moisture, pain, swelling, injury, foreign body possibility, and age-appropriate sexual history. Use neutral, nonleading questions and follow mandatory-reporting requirements when abuse is suspected.

Part 3 — Collect Urine Before Treatment When Safe

The collection method determines how confidently a culture can diagnose infection. For a toilet-trained child, use a careful clean-catch midstream specimen. For a non-toilet-trained child who needs definitive culture, catheterization or another validated low-contamination method is generally required by the applicable pathway.

Bag specimens have high false-positive culture rates and should not establish UTI. A conveniently collected specimen may support screening urinalysis in selected circumstances, but a positive result should lead to a reliable culture specimen. Document the method.

Part 4 — Interpret Urinalysis and Culture Together

Pyuria, leukocyte esterase, nitrites, microscopy, symptoms, fever, collection method, organism, and colony pattern all matter. Nitrite is specific when positive but may be negative when urine has not remained in the bladder long enough or with organisms that do not reduce nitrate. Absence of one marker does not replace clinical judgment.

Mixed organisms or low-count growth from a poor-quality specimen often indicates contamination. Bacteriuria without symptoms and inflammation is not automatically a UTI and generally should not trigger antibiotics in otherwise healthy children. Reconcile the culture when it returns and stop or narrow therapy when appropriate.

Part 5 — Lower Versus Upper Tract Disease

Cystitis more often causes dysuria, urgency, frequency, and suprapubic discomfort without systemic illness. Fever, flank pain, vomiting, ill appearance, or elevated inflammatory response raises concern for pyelonephritis or another serious process. Infants may not localize.

Choose antibiotics using prior cultures, age, allergy, kidney function, local susceptibility, illness severity, and ability to take oral medication. Do not use a drug with poor renal-tissue penetration for suspected pyelonephritis. Arrange culture review and clinical reassessment.

Part 6 — Imaging and Recurrent UTI

Imaging after febrile UTI depends on age, recurrence, clinical course, organism, prenatal findings, family history, and current pediatric guidance. Renal and bladder ultrasound evaluates anatomy but does not diagnose reflux. Voiding cystourethrography is selective rather than automatic for every first infection.

Recurrent UTI requires confirmation that prior episodes were true infections, review of specimen quality and susceptibility, and assessment of constipation, withholding, dysfunctional elimination, reflux or obstruction, stones, and sexual exposure. Repeated empiric antibiotics without this reconstruction increases harm.

Part 7 — Bowel-Bladder Dysfunction

Constipation and voiding dysfunction commonly drive frequency, urgency, daytime wetting, recurrent symptoms, and UTI risk. Ask stool frequency, painful or large stools, encopresis, withholding postures, toilet access, school bathroom avoidance, fluid intake, and timed voiding.

Treatment may include constipation management, scheduled relaxed voiding, hydration, proper posture, and positive reinforcement. Avoid punishment. Persistent weak stream, straining, continuous dribbling, recurrent febrile UTI, neurologic signs, or abnormal spine examination requires urologic or neurologic evaluation.

Part 8 — Enuresis

Primary monosymptomatic nocturnal enuresis occurs in a child who has never achieved sustained nighttime dryness and has no daytime urinary symptoms. Secondary enuresis follows at least six months of dryness and raises questions about stress, constipation, UTI, diabetes, sleep-disordered breathing, seizure, trauma, or neurologic disease.

Assess daytime symptoms and constipation before labeling the condition. Urinalysis is often the focused initial test; extensive imaging is not routine for uncomplicated monosymptomatic enuresis. Treatment can include education, fluid and voiding routines, alarm therapy, and selected medication after shared decision-making.

Part 9 — Vulvovaginal Symptoms

Prepubertal vulvovaginitis often reflects moisture, irritants, hygiene, tight clothing, or nonspecific inflammation. Examine externally with consent and a chaperone according to policy. Avoid internal examination in a routine prepubertal evaluation. Provide gentle hygiene, avoidance of fragranced products, breathable clothing, and treatment targeted to a confirmed cause.

Persistent foul or bloody discharge raises concern for foreign body or other pathology. Genital injury, STI, disclosure, behavioral concern, or examination findings inconsistent with history requires a trauma-informed child-protection pathway; do not conduct repeated interviews.

Part 10 — Balanitis and Foreskin Care

Balanitis may result from irritation, infection, or poor local hygiene. Assess pain, swelling, discharge, voiding, diabetes risk, and paraphimosis. The foreskin of a young child may be physiologically nonretractile; do not forcibly retract it. Teach gentle external cleansing.

Paraphimosis—retracted foreskin trapped behind the glans with swelling—is an urgent urologic problem. Inability to urinate, ischemic color change, severe pain, or rapidly increasing swelling requires emergency care.

Part 11 — Acute Scrotal Pain

Testicular torsion is a time-sensitive emergency. Sudden severe unilateral pain, nausea or vomiting, high-riding or transverse testis, swelling, or absent cremasteric reflex increases concern, but no single finding safely excludes it. Adolescents may describe only abdominal pain.

Do not delay urologic consultation for routine outpatient imaging when clinical suspicion is high. Epididymitis, torsion of an appendage, hernia, trauma, tumor, and infection remain in the differential, but testicular viability depends on rapid action.

Part 12 — Hematuria and Proteinuria

Confirm whether urine is truly bloody and distinguish red cells from hemoglobin, myoglobin, foods, or medications. Ask dysuria, fever, flank pain, trauma, exercise, recent infection, edema, rash, joint symptoms, hearing loss, and family renal disease. Measure blood pressure and assess edema and renal function when indicated.

Transient microscopic hematuria or proteinuria may resolve, but persistence, gross hematuria, hypertension, edema, reduced kidney function, significant protein, casts, or systemic symptoms requires prompt nephrology-oriented evaluation. Cola-colored urine with edema and hypertension suggests glomerular disease rather than cystitis.

Part 13 — Close the Culture and Result Loop

Before the patient leaves, document the pending culture owner, expected time, contact method, and actions for susceptible, resistant, mixed, or negative results. Confirm that symptoms improve. A family should not continue an unnecessary antibiotic because no one reviewed a negative culture.

Clinical Case 1 — Bag Culture Confusion

A febrile 14-month-old has a bag culture growing mixed organisms. The FNP recognizes likely contamination, reassesses severity, and obtains a reliable urinalysis and culture specimen before changing antibiotics when clinically safe.

Clinical Case 2 — Wetting and Constipation

An eight-year-old has urgency, daytime accidents, hard stools, and several prior “UTIs” without documented cultures. The FNP reconstructs the episodes, assesses bowel-bladder dysfunction, treats constipation and voiding habits, and reserves antibiotics for confirmed infection.

Clinical Case 3 — Abdominal Pain Is Torsion

A 15-year-old with sudden lower-abdominal pain and vomiting privately reports unilateral scrotal pain. The FNP performs an urgent focused examination and arranges immediate emergency urologic evaluation without delaying for a routine appointment.

FNP High-Yield Framework: URINE

  1. U — Urgency first: sepsis, obstruction, torsion, paraphimosis, trauma, renal compromise.
  2. R — Reliable specimen: collection method, urinalysis, culture before antibiotics when safe.
  3. I — Integrate the pattern: lower versus upper tract, bowel-bladder, genital, STI, glomerular.
  4. N — Narrow treatment: prior cultures, local resistance, tissue penetration, culture reconciliation.
  5. E — Ensure follow-up: clinical response, imaging when indicated, referral and result ownership.

Take-Home Summary

Pediatric urinary care depends on specimen quality and pattern recognition. A bag culture cannot establish UTI; constipation can drive recurrent urinary symptoms; blood and protein require blood-pressure and renal context; and sudden scrotal pain is a surgical emergency until torsion is excluded.

Educational note: Use current local pediatric UTI, antimicrobial, imaging, STI, child-protection, and emergency protocols. Toxic appearance, young-infant fever, obstructed urine, shock, acute scrotal pain, paraphimosis, genital trauma, severe hypertension, edema with renal dysfunction, or safeguarding concern requires urgent evaluation.
